prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "LOCKHEED MARTIN CORP" (ticker LMT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "LMT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
markets: Combat aircraft and sustainment (F-35, F-16, F-22 support, C-130J)
Missiles, missile defense and fire control (PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, JASSM/LRASM, GMLRS, PrSM, HIMARS, Javelin with RTX)
Helicopters and mission systems (Sikorsky Black Hawk, CH-53K, Aegis, radars, C2)
Space systems (Orion, GPS III, missile-warning and tracking satellites, Trident II D5 fleet ballistic missiles, Next Generation Interceptor)
Hypersonics, counter-drone and space-based interceptors (Golden Dome)

mission.plain: Build the planes, missiles, satellites and systems that help the US and its allies keep people safe.

about.plain: Lockheed Martin is the world's biggest defense company. It builds the F-35 stealth fighter jet, Black Hawk helicopters, missiles that shoot down other missiles, and satellites such as GPS. Almost all of its customers are governments, mainly the US military. It also keeps the jets and systems it sold working for decades by supplying parts, upgrades and repairs.
about.customers: The US government (72% of 2025 sales, mostly the military) and about 28% from allied governments abroad.
about.everyday: The GPS satellites that help phone maps find your location are built by Lockheed Martin, and it built NASA's Orion capsule that carries astronauts around the Moon.

money.plain: F-35 and F-16 fighters, C-130J cargo planes and their upkeep; the F-35 alone was 27% of 2025 sales
Sikorsky helicopters, ship combat systems like Aegis, radars
PAC-3 and THAAD interceptors, GMLRS rockets, HIMARS launchers, JASSM cruise missiles
satellites, Orion spacecraft, Trident submarine missiles, missile interceptors

money.part: Golden Dome space-based interceptors and missile defense
money.plain: prototype interceptors in orbit to stop missiles aimed at the US

money.part: Counter-drone and undersea autonomy (Sanctum, planned Ultra Maritime purchase)
money.plain: systems that knock down cheap drones and sensors and drones for submarine hunting

result.summary: Lockheed Martin has a strong competitive advantage rooted in sole-source franchises the US and its allies cannot easily replace: the F-35 is the only Western fifth-generation fighter in production, and PAC-3 MSE and THAAD are core to allied missile defense. Classified know-how, security clearances, decades-long sustainment contracts and a record $230.4B backlog (June 2026) make it very hard to dislodge. Its weakness is that it sells mostly to one powerful buyer on cost-plus or fixed-price terms, which caps margins and has produced large program charges.

pricingPower.evidence: The US government sets prices through negotiated cost-plus and fixed-price contracts, so margins are thin and falling: gross margin was 13.2% in 2020 but 10.2% in 2025 ($7,619M on $75,048M sales), and fixed-price programs caused $1,615M of segment losses in 2025 (a $950M classified Aeronautics program, $570M Canadian Maritime Helicopter, $95M Turkish Utility Helicopter); demand, however, is rising, with backlog up from $193.6B at end-2025 to $230.4B in June 2026.

moats.evidence: Lockheed Martin and Skunk Works carry unmatched credibility with defense ministries (F-35, F-22, SR-71, U-2 heritage), and the company owns key designs, IP and certified production lines for programs like PAC-3 and THAAD.

Countries that buy the F-35 depend on Lockheed for parts, software upgrades and sustainment for 40+ years, and the US Government's program of record is 2,456 F-35s plus allied orders; switching fighter fleets takes decades and billions.
Each additional F-35 or Patriot/PAC-3 nation strengthens interoperability and shared logistics among allies, which makes the platform more attractive to the next buyer.

It is the largest defense contractor by defense revenue ($75.0B in 2025) and delivered a record 191 F-35s in 2025, spreading fixed costs across very long production runs, though cost-plus pricing passes much of that benefit to the customer.

Markets such as fifth-generation fighters, ballistic missile interceptors (THAAD, PAC-3 MSE) and fleet ballistic missiles (Trident II D5) support only one supplier, so a new entrant cannot earn a return.
Lockheed is the incumbent; venture-backed rivals such as Anduril and SpaceX counter-position against it with cheaper, faster, software-led products.
Stealth coatings, sensor fusion, hit-to-kill interceptor seekers and Skunk Works rapid prototyping reflect decades of classified know-how that rivals cannot copy quickly.
About 72,000 of its roughly 123,000 employees are engineers, scientists and IT staff, many with security clearances, and it holds classified programs and export approvals few firms can access.

customers.evidence: Customers keep coming back: the Missile Defense Agency awarded a seven-year, $35 billion contract in 2026 to quadruple THAAD interceptor production, the Army signed a $3 billion GMLRS deal, and backlog hit a record $230.4B (3.2-to-1 book-to-bill in Q2 2026), though some partners have complained about F-35 delays and sustainment costs.

talent.evidence: It employs about 123,000 people including about 72,000 engineers, scientists and IT professionals and was named one of Canada's Most Attractive Employers in 2023, but it competes for engineers with SpaceX, Anduril and big tech, which pay more and are seen as more exciting.

product.evidence: The F-35 is the only fifth-generation fighter in production in the West and a record 191 were delivered in 2025, while PAC-3 MSE and THAAD are combat-proven ballistic missile interceptors; reliability, software (TR-3/Block 4) delays and cost overruns are the main criticisms.

competitors.name: RTX Corporation (Raytheon)
competitors.note: Missiles and air defense (Patriot system vs PAC-3 interceptor partner, SM-6, Tomahawk, AMRAAM), radars, hypersonics; partner on Javelin and supplier of the F-35's F135 engine.

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman
competitors.note: B-21 bomber, space systems and missile-warning satellites, Sentinel ICBM, missile defense (IBCS, GBI), and F-35 center fuselage supplier.

competitors.name: The Boeing Company (Defense, Space & Security)
competitors.note: Fighters (F-15EX, F-47 sixth-generation fighter win), helicopters (Apache, Chinook), satellites, and a partner in United Launch Alliance; also supplies PAC-3 seekers.

competitors.name: General Dynamics
competitors.note: Mission systems, C4ISR and IT services for the US government; also combat vehicles and submarines.

competitors.name: L3Harris Technologies
competitors.note: Space sensors and missile-tracking satellites, electronic warfare, communications, and rocket motors (Aerojet Rocketdyne).

competitors.name: Anduril Industries
competitors.note: Venture-backed challenger in autonomous aircraft (CCA), counter-drone systems, low-cost missiles and space surveillance.

competitors.name: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX)
competitors.note: National-security launches, Starshield satellites and proliferated satellite constellations for the Space Development Agency; a contender for Golden Dome work.

competitors.name: BAE Systems
competitors.note: Eurofighter and GCAP/Tempest fighters, electronic warfare (also an F-35 partner), munitions and combat systems.

competitors.name: Airbus (Defence and Space)
competitors.note: Eurofighter partner, FCAS future fighter, A400M vs C-130J, military satellites and helicopters.

competitors.name: Dassault Aviation
competitors.note: Rafale fighter competes with the F-35 and F-16 in export fighter competitions.

competitors.name: Saab
competitors.note: Gripen fighter vs F-16/F-35 exports, radars, missiles and naval systems.

competitors.name: MBDA
competitors.note: European missile maker (Airbus, BAE, Leonardo) competing with PAC-3 and JASSM via SAMP/T Aster and cruise missiles.

competitors.name: Leonardo
competitors.note: Helicopters (vs Sikorsky), defense electronics and GCAP fighter partner; also an F-35 final assembly partner in Italy.

competitors.name: Textron (Bell)
competitors.note: Bell V-280 won the Army's long-range assault aircraft competition against the Sikorsky-Boeing Defiant X.

competitors.name: Rheinmetall
competitors.note: Air defense, munitions and rocket artillery in Europe; also a partner for European missile production.

estimates.name: BAE Systems (estimate; not an SEC filer)
Airbus SE (estimate, converted from EUR 73.4B at about 1.13 USD/EUR; whole group)

threats: Dependence on one buyer: 72% of 2025 sales came from the US government, so budget fights, continuing resolutions or shutdowns can delay orders and cash.
F-35 concentration (27% of 2025 sales): cuts to planned buys, TR-3/Block 4 software delays or allied preference for European fighters (FCAS, GCAP) would hurt.
Fixed-price development contracts have caused large losses ($1,615M of segment losses in 2025) and could do so again.
Cheaper, faster, software-led challengers (Anduril, SpaceX, Palantir-style integrators) and Pentagon acquisition reform favoring commercial and attritable systems.
Losing next-generation competitions (Boeing won the Air Force's F-47 sixth-generation fighter; Bell won the Army's long-range assault aircraft) erodes future franchises.
Execution risk in quadrupling THAAD and ramping PAC-3 MSE output, where large ramps dilute margins; plus ULA launch issues weighing on Space profits.

ceo.name: James D. (Jim) Taiclet
ceo.background: US Air Force Academy engineering and international relations graduate, Princeton master's, former Air Force C-141 pilot; previously chairman, president and CEO of American Tower, and executive at Honeywell (AlliedSignal) and Pratt & Whitney

c1.evidence: Lockheed leads defense aerospace, a mature industry that grew sales only from $65,398M in 2020 to $75,048M in 2025 (about 3% a year), not an emerging fast-growth one.

c2.evidence: Governments choose it for unique, combat-proven products (F-35, PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, Trident II D5) backed by classified know-how and 40-year sustainment ties, an advantage that is very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: The name is widely recognised and it is the default leader in defense (the world's largest defense contractor), but ordinary people do not use its products and opinions about weapons makers are mixed.

c4.evidence: Its stated purpose is to deliver the capabilities that help America and its allies stay 'ahead of ready', which matters for national security, but management is a professional, financially driven team rather than a mission-obsessed founder group.

c6.evidence: “F-35, defense contractor, military-industrial complex” come to mind; the impression is respected for engineering but mixed, as many associate it with weapons, cost overruns and government spending.

c7.evidence: Global defense spending is rising (NATO's higher spending targets, US proposals to lift the defense budget, missile-defense restocking and Golden Dome), but it is a large, government-funded market growing in single digits, not a secular tech trend like AI.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into space-based interceptors for Golden Dome, counter-drone systems (Sanctum), undersea autonomy (agreed $3.45B Ultra Maritime purchase) and European missile production with Rheinmetall, but all within defense.

m1.evidence: Taiclet has pushed a '21st Century Security' vision of networked, digitally connected forces and bet ahead of demand on munitions capacity, but he is more a disciplined operator than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Taiclet is a hired CEO who joined in June 2020 after running American Tower, not a founder.

m4.evidence: As a former Air Force pilot he speaks often about serving the warfighter and customers, but there is no clear evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style toward employees.

m5.evidence: Skunk Works and rapid efforts like the Sanctum counter-drone system (concept to live-fire in under 45 days) show an inventive culture, but much of that culture predates Taiclet and the firm also suffered large program overruns.

m6.evidence: Taiclet holds an engineering degree from the Air Force Academy and flew 5,000+ hours, but his career has been mostly in management and finance-oriented leadership (American Tower).

m7.evidence: He frames the company's work around deterring war and protecting allies, with no known scandals, but stewardship focuses on national security and shareholder returns rather than humanity broadly.

m7b.evidence: No commencement address by Jim Taiclet at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Taiclet is a low-profile, conventional corporate CEO rather than a memorable public personality.

m9.evidence: Under Taiclet backlog grew to a record $230.4B (June 2026) and free cash flow reached $6,908M in 2025, but operating margin fell from 13.6% in 2021 to 10.3% in 2025 after large fixed-price program losses.

m10.evidence: Lockheed is not known for frugality; it is a large contractor whose costs are largely reimbursed by the government.

c10.evidence: GPS satellites it builds help billions navigate and its missile defenses protect civilians from attacks, but most of its products are weapons used by militaries rather than everyday tools.

p2.evidence: Stealth fighters, hit-to-kill interceptors like THAAD and PAC-3, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and the Orion deep-space capsule are among the hardest engineering feats and matter for national security.

f1.evidence: Sales rose in four of the last five years ($65,398M in 2020 to $75,048M in 2025) but fell in 2022 to $65,984M from $67,044M.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 13.2% in 2020 to 10.2% in 2025 and operating margin from 13.2% to 10.3%, hit by program losses.

f3.evidence: Debt of $20,538M far exceeds $3,791M of cash (June 2026) but is about 2.4x 2025 operating cash flow of $8,557M, and shareholders' equity is positive at $8,768M.

f4.evidence: Operating profit fell from $8,644M in 2020 to $7,731M in 2025, while operating cash flow was roughly flat ($8,183M in 2020, $8,557M in 2025) with a dip to $6,972M in 2024.

v1.evidence: The F-35 is the only stealth fighter allies can buy, combining stealth, sensors and data sharing no rival export fighter matches, which is why countries from Poland to Japan pick it.

v2.evidence: It is a respected, mission-driven employer (named among Canada's Most Attractive Employers in 2023) with about 72,000 engineers and scientists, but it is not a fixture on top 'best companies to work for' lists like Fortune's 100 Best.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, the US and allied militaries would lose F-35 support, THAAD and PAC-3 interceptors, GPS satellites and Trident missiles, weakening deterrence; whether weapons make the world better is debated.
